title: The Acquisition Is the Easy Part. Financing It Without Straining the Rest of the Business Isn't.
linkedin:
Most owners spend weeks working out what to buy. They spend a single phone call working out how to fund it.

That gap is where a lot of otherwise sound bolt-on acquisitions get into trouble. Not because the target was wrong. Because the purchase price and the cost of actually running two businesses together got treated as the same number.

They are not.

The purchase price buys the business. A second, usually overlooked number carries it through the months where two systems run in parallel, staff sit across both sites while roles get sorted out, and the acquired business's own debtor days have not yet settled into the parent's rhythm. That second number needs cash in the weeks right after settlement, the worst possible time to discover the funding plan never covered it.

Vendor finance gets the same treatment, as a negotiating outcome rather than a financing decision. Priced properly, a seller who accepts part of the price over time is often the most patient capital in the whole deal. Priced casually, as a number agreed just to close, it becomes a second, forgotten instalment landing right as integration costs hit.

The businesses that come through an acquisition cleanly are the ones that priced both of these properly before signing, not after.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

Ever bought something for the business and only really felt the cost of owning it a few months later? Buying another business works the same way, just with a lot more zeros.

Most owners get the purchase price sorted. What catches them out is everything after settlement: running two systems at once, staff spread across two sites, chasing the new business's invoices until its collections fall into rhythm. None of that shows up in the contract, and all of it needs cash exactly when the excitement of the deal has worn off.

Thinking about buying a competitor or a complementary business this year? Genuinely curious how far along that thinking is for people reading this.

Thinking about growing by buying another business rather than building organically? It is one of the fastest ways an Australian SME adds revenue, a client book or a second location, and it is also where a lot of otherwise solid deals quietly get into trouble.

The mistake is rarely the target chosen. It is treating the purchase price as the whole funding number. Running two systems in parallel, carrying staff across both sites while roles settle, and covering the acquired business's own debtor days until collections normalise all draw on cash in the weeks right after settlement, separate from the price paid for the business itself.

Vendor finance, where a seller accepts part of the price over time, is worth taking seriously too. Priced properly it can be the most patient capital available. Priced casually, it becomes a second bill landing at the worst possible time.

If a bolt-on acquisition is on the table for your business this year in Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales or Victoria, it is worth getting the funding structure tested before the offer goes in, not after. Read the full piece on the blog.
